question: We're playing best of five games to 11. In the third game, when do we switch ends?

answer.reasoning: The question describes a best-of-five-games-to-11 match, which matches the Alternative Laws format 'best-of-5-games-11'. I searched for the change-of-ends rules and found the standard Law 8.1.3 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) and the alternative clauses for the best-of-5-games-11 format (Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, in force 2027-01-04). The standard rule says ends change in the third game when a side first scores 11 points; the alternative format instead changes ends at the end of the third game if there is a fourth game, with the only mid-game change in that format being in the fifth game at 6 points. Both together answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: Under the standard Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), Law 8.1.3, players change ends "in the third game when a side first scores 11 points, except in Handicap Matches (BWF Statute Section 4.1.3)". However, your match — best of five games to 11 — is the Alternative Laws format 'best-of-5-games-11' (Alternative Laws of Badminton 2.0, in force 2027-01-04). In that format there is no mid-game change of ends in the third game: players change ends "at the end of the third game, if there is to be a fourth game". The only mid-game change of ends in the best-of-5-games-11 format is "in the fifth game when a side first scores 6 points".

question: My opponent shouted 'fault!' while I was playing my shot. What's the ruling?

answer.reasoning: The question asks about an opponent shouting 'fault!' during the user's shot. Two sources bear directly: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 13.4.5 makes deliberately distracting an opponent by shouting a fault 'in play', and Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.4 explicitly states that a player calling 'fault' to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke is a deliberate distraction under Law 13.4.5. Law 7.3 gives the consequence: the side winning a rally (here, by the opponent's fault) adds a point. ITTO 5.9.1.3 is a contrast case (shouting to one's own partner is not necessarily distraction) and does not apply since the shout was directed at the opponent. Together the sources answer the question fully.
answer.answer: It is a fault by your opponent. Under Law 13.4.5 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) (in force 2025-04-26), it is a fault if, in play, a player 'deliberately distracts an opponent by any action such as shouting or making gestures'. The Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) (in force 2025-04-26), clause 5.9.1.4, make this specific: 'A player calling 'fault', etc. to the opponent when making a stroke or after the opponent has made a stroke, shall be considered a deliberate distraction (Law 13.4.5)'. Because your opponent committed a fault, your side wins the rally, and under Law 7.3 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) 'The side winning a rally shall add a point to its score' — the shuttle ceases to be in play because of the fault. (Note: by contrast, ITTO 7.0 (5) clause 5.9.1.3 says shouting to one's own partner who is about to hit the shuttle is not necessarily a deliberate distraction of the opponents — but that does not apply here, since the shout was directed at you.)

question: When do we replay a rally? List every situation that counts as a let.

answer.reasoning: The question asks for every situation that counts as a let and when a rally is replayed. Law 14 (LETS) of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, is the governing clause: 14.1 says who calls a let, 14.2 lists all let situations (14.2.1–14.2.7, with 14.2.3 expanded into 14.2.3.1 and 14.2.3.2), and 14.3 states the effect (the rally is replayed). Law 17.6.6 also provides for playing a let when an appointed official is unsighted. The para-only clause 14.2.3.2.1 is omitted because the question is not about para play. Together these sources fully answer the question.
answer.answer: A rally is replayed whenever a 'let' is called. Under Law 14 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26: "'Let' shall be called by the umpire, or by a player (if there is no umpire), to halt play" (Law 14.1), and "When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again" (Law 14.3) — i.e., the rally is replayed from the last service. Law 14.2 lists every situation that is a let: (1) the server serves before the receiver is ready (Law 9.4) [14.2.1]; (2) during service, the receiver and the server are both faulted [14.2.2]; (3) after the service is returned, the shuttle is caught on the net and remains suspended on its top [14.2.3.1]; (4) after the service is returned, after passing over the net the shuttle is caught in the net [14.2.3.2]; (5) during play, the shuttle disintegrates and the base completely separates from the rest of the shuttle [14.2.4]; (6) in the opinion of the umpire, play is disrupted or a player of the opposing side is distracted by a coach [14.2.5]; (7) a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision [14.2.6]; (8) any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred [14.2.7]. Additionally, under Law 17.6.6, where an appointed official is unsighted, the umpire carries out that official's duties or plays a 'let'.

question: My partner cut his hand mid-game and it's bleeding. How long can we stop, and who can come on court to help?

answer.reasoning: The question asks two things: the permitted length of a stoppage for a bleeding injury, and who may enter the court to help. The Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) cover suspension of play generally (laws-16.3.1, laws-16.3.3), and the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5) cover injuries specifically: itto-5.14.2 addresses blood-flowing injuries directly, itto-3.6.1.4 gives the time expectation ('well within a few minutes'), itto-5.14.1 has the Umpire timing the delay and the Referee deciding who comes on court, itto-3.6.1.1 says the Referee and Tournament Doctor go on court when called, itto-3.6.1.3 caps assistants at two persons, and itto-3.6.1.2 allows only quick relief such as a bandage. Together these answer both parts; nothing is missing.
answer.answer: How long you can stop: there is no fixed time limit. Under Law 16.3.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), 'When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary,' and under Law 16.3.3 'the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point.' For a bleeding injury specifically, Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), Clause 5.14.2, says: 'For a blood flowing injury, the game should be delayed until the bleeding stops, the wound is suitably dressed, or the Referee advises the Umpire otherwise.' The Referee must resolve the situation 'as quickly as possible and well within a few minutes so that play can be resumed or abandoned' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.6.1.4), the Umpire times the delay (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.14.1: 'The Umpire shall time the delay caused by the injury'), and 'No treatment causing undue delay shall be given on court' (same clause). The Tournament Doctor 'may apply a quick relief, such as a bandage on a bleeding injury, but no time-consuming treatment is allowed except in the regular intervals' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.6.1.2). Who may come on court: when the Umpire calls, 'the Referee and the Tournament Doctor shall immediately go on court' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.6.1.1), and 'The Referee will decide whether the Tournament Doctor or anyone else is required on court' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.14.1). Beyond that, 'The Referee may allow a maximum of two persons on court to assist and advise the injured player and help with translation. In fairness, the Referee shall allow the opposing side the same consideration' (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 3.6.1.3).

question: Water started dripping from the roof onto our court mid-game. What happens to the match and the score?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to a match and score when water drips onto the court mid-game. Two rule situations apply: (1) if the court becomes temporarily not playable, play is suspended — ITTO 5.11.2 and 5.11.3 cover circumstances affecting playing conditions and courts needing repair, and Laws 16.3.1/16.3.3 cover suspension and the score; (2) if it happens during a rally as an unforeseen/accidental situation, it is a 'let' under Law 14.2.7, and Law 14.3 says the rally does not count. Together these answer both the match and the score. No para-badminton rule is needed since this is not a para question.
answer.answer:
Water dripping onto the court is a circumstance not within the players' control, so two things can happen depending on severity:

1. Suspension of play (if the court or its immediate surroundings is temporarily not playable): Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.3.1, "When necessitated by circumstances not within the control of the players, the umpire may suspend play for such a period as the umpire may consider necessary." Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.11.2, "Play may be suspended by the Referee or Umpire if warranted by a circumstance affecting playing conditions," and Clause 5.11.3: "If, during a match, a court or its immediate surroundings needs repair, or it is temporarily not playable, the Umpire shall call the Referee (or the Referee shall go onto the court) and play be suspended until the court and its immediate surroundings are again suitable for play." When play is suspended, the Umpire calls "Play is suspended" and notes "S" on the scoring device or score-sheet (ITTO 5.11.4). When play resumes, the Umpire notes the duration of the suspension, ensures the players are on the correct side of the net and in the correct service courts, then calls "Are you ready?" followed by the score and "Play" (ITTO 5.11.5).

2. Let (if it disrupts a rally): Under the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), Law 14.2.7, it shall be a 'let' if "any unforeseen or accidental situation has occurred."

The score: in either case the score does not change. For a suspension, Law 16.3.3 states: "If play is suspended, the existing score shall stand and play shall be resumed from that point." For a let, Law 14.3 states: "When a 'let' occurs, play since the last service shall not count and the player who served last shall serve again" — so no point is awarded and the same score is announced when play resumes.

question: My opponent keeps flicking sweat onto the court. What can the umpire do about it?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what the umpire can do when a player flicks sweat onto the court. The Instructions to Technical Officials contain a clause directly on point: ITTO 5.9.1.6 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26) says a player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court must be reminded the conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied if necessary. Law 16.7.1 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) sets out the escalation the umpire administers for a breach of Law 16.6: a warning (16.7.1.1), a fault if previously warned (16.7.1.2), or a fault for a flagrant offence (16.7.1.3). ITTO 5.17.3 describes the warning procedure (yellow card, 'warning for misconduct'). Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: Throwing sweat onto the court is specifically covered. Under the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 5.9.1.6: 'A player throwing sweat or otherwise contaminating the court and its immediate surroundings shall be reminded that such conduct is unacceptable, with Law 16.7 applied, if necessary'. If it continues, the umpire administers the breach under Law 16.7.1 of the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, which allows the umpire to: issue a warning to the offending side (Law 16.7.1.1); fault the offending side if previously warned (Law 16.7.1.2); or fault the offending side in cases of flagrant offence or breach (Law 16.7.1.3). The warning is delivered per ITTO 5.17.3 by calling the player over and calling 'warning for misconduct' while raising a yellow card above the head. The underlying misconduct provision is Law 16.6 (a player shall not 'behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner' (16.6.3) or 'be guilty of misconduct not otherwise covered by the Laws of Badminton' (16.6.4)), which is one of the Laws whose breach Law 16.7.1 covers.

question: The line judge couldn't see whether the shuttle landed in. What happens to the rally?

answer.reasoning: The question asks what happens to the rally when a line judge could not see whether the shuttle landed in. The sources cover this directly: itto-8.5 tells the line judge what to do when unsighted; itto-2.5 and itto-5.8.3 say the umpire then makes the call; laws-14.2.6, itto-2.5 and itto-5.8.3.3 say that if neither the umpire nor the Instant Review System can decide, the rally is a 'let'. answer.answer: If the line judge could not see the shuttle land, the line judge must immediately signal "unsighted" to the umpire by putting both hands up to cover the eyes (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, Clause 8.5: "If unsighted, inform the Umpire immediately by putting both hands up to cover the eyes."). The umpire then makes the decision: "When another official is unsighted, the Umpire shall make the decision" (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 2.5), and "Where there is no Line Judge or if a Line Judge is unsighted, the Umpire shall immediately call" the appropriate call (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 5.8.3) — "Out" if the shuttle landed outside the line, or "Let" followed by the score if the umpire is also unsighted (ITTO 7.0 (5), Clauses 5.8.3.1 and 5.8.3.3). If no decision can be made — i.e. the line judge is unsighted and the umpire or the Instant Review System is unable to make a decision — it is a "let" and the rally is replayed: Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 14.2.6: "a line judge is unsighted and the umpire or Instant Review System is unable to make a decision; or"; and ITTO 7.0 (5), Clause 2.5: "When no decision can be made, a 'let' shall be called (Law 17.6.6), unless IRS is in use, in which case it will be used to decide on the line call". So the rally either gets a decision from the umpire (or IRS), or it is a let.

question: Can my coach get up from his chair and stand at the side of the court during the match?

answer.reasoning: The question asks whether a coach may stand at the side of the court during a match. The Instructions to Technical Officials clause 5.12.2 (Coaching from Off Court) directly answers this: coaches must be seated in designated seats and must not stand court-side during the match except during permitted intervals. Law 16.2 defines those permitted intervals (60 seconds at 11 points in each game; 120 seconds between games), and ITTO 5.12.1 adds that coaching is not allowed while the shuttle is in play. Together these fully answer the question, so no refusal is needed.
answer.answer: No. During the match your coach must stay seated in his designated seat and must not stand court-side, except during the permitted intervals. The permitted intervals are: not exceeding 60 seconds during each game when the leading score reaches 11 points, and not exceeding 120 seconds between the first and second game and between the second and third game. In addition, coaching is not allowed from the moment the players have taken up position to serve and receive the next service, and while the shuttle is in play. (Rules from the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26, clause 5.12.2 and 5.12.1, and the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, Law 16.2.1 and 16.2.2.)

question: What weight range is allowed for a plastic shuttle, and since our hall gets really hot and stuffy in summer, can we use a special type made for hot weather?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) the allowed weight of a plastic (non-feathered/synthetic) shuttle, and (2) whether a special hot-weather shuttle type exists. Laws 2.2.6 and 2.3.3 (Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26) answer the weight part: the standard shuttle weight is 4.74–5.50 g, and for a non-feathered (synthetic/plastic) shuttle a variation of up to 10 per cent is acceptable. Law 2.4 answers the hot-weather part: there is no special 'hot weather' shuttle type in the Laws; instead, modifications to the specifications may be made with the approval of the Member Association concerned where atmospheric conditions due to altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable, subject to no variation in general design, speed and flight. ITTO 3.5.4.7 is also relevant context: shuttles may need retesting when temperature/humidity change substantially, but that concerns testing, not a special shuttle type. Together the sources answer both parts of the question.
answer.answer: Weight: A plastic shuttle is a 'Non-Feathered Shuttle' under Law 2.3. Its measurements and weight must be as in Laws 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.6 — i.e. the shuttle shall weigh from 4.74 to 5.50 grams — but because of the difference in specific gravity and other properties of synthetic materials compared with feathers, a variation of up to 10 per cent is acceptable (Law 2.3.3). So the base range is 4.74–5.50 g, with up to 10% variation allowed for plastic/synthetic shuttles (which works out to roughly 4.27–6.05 g). Hot weather: The Laws do not define a special 'hot weather' shuttle type. What Law 2.4 allows is that, subject to there being no variation in the general design, speed and flight of the shuttle, modifications in the specifications may be made with the approval of the Member Association concerned, in places where atmospheric conditions due to either altitude or climate make the standard shuttle unsuitable. So for a hot, stuffy hall you would need a Member-Association-approved modification of the standard shuttle, not a separate off-the-shelf 'hot weather' model under the Laws. Separately, the Instructions to Technical Officials note that shuttles should be retested if playing conditions change substantially (e.g. temperature and humidity). All rules cited are from the Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2), in force 2025-04-26, except the retesting point, which is from the Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26.

question: My opponent got a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before the umpire called 'Play'. Does it cost him a point now, and does the card go on his record after the tournament?

answer.reasoning: The question has two parts: (1) whether a yellow card for swearing during the warm-up, before 'Play', costs a point now, and (2) whether the card goes on the player's record after the tournament. The sources answer both directly. ITTO 5.17.10 (Instructions to Technical Officials 7.0 (5), in force 2025-04-26) expressly covers misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before 'Play' is called: any card given has no effect on the score but is taken into account if further offences occur during the match. Laws of Badminton 5.0 (2) Law 16.6.3 makes offensive/inappropriate behaviour a breach, Law 16.7.1.1 provides the warning (yellow card) as the first sanction, and Law 16.7.1.2 provides faulting only if previously warned. ITTO 5.17.3 describes the yellow-card procedure. For the record question, ITTO 3.7.3 requires the Referee to send BWF (or CC) a report on yellow and red cards after the tournament that may trigger further sanctions. The question's assumption (warm-up before 'Play' = before the match) matches the condition in ITTO 5.17.10, so no correction is needed.
answer.answer: No, the yellow card does not cost him a point now. Misconduct before the match while on the Field of Play before 'Play' has been called is still carded (as a warning under Law 16.7.1.1, shown as a yellow card per ITTO 5.17.3), but per ITTO 5.17.10 'Any card(s) given shall have no effect on the score of the match' — the only consequence is that the card 'shall be taken into account if further offences occur during the match' (Law 16.7.1.2), meaning a further offence would lead to a fault (red card) rather than another warning. Swearing is a breach of Law 16.6.3 ('behave in an offensive or inappropriate manner'). As for the record: yes, the card does not disappear at the end of the tournament — ITTO 3.7.3 requires that 'The Referee shall immediately after the tournament send to BWF (or CC) a report on withdrawals, yellow and red cards, that may trigger further sanctions.' So the yellow card is reported to BWF (or the relevant CC) after the tournament and may trigger further sanctions.
